title: Ethics Advisory Opinion No. 25-045-E
summary: A former state agency employee may be retained as a service provider to the same office of the agency in which he or she was previously employed as long as the former employee was not personally or directly involved in the particular application, and no violation of Section 25-4-105(3)(e), Miss. Code of 1972, is likely to occur. However, the former employee may have gained nonpublic information which could be used in violation of Section 25-4-105(5), and an appearance of impropriety could arise under Section 25-4-101. Those concerns could prompt the state agency to deny the application of this former employee.

ETHICS ADVISORY OPINION NO. 25-045-E
January 9, 2026
Question Presented: May a former state agency employee be retained as a service
provider to the same office of the agency in which he or she was
previously employed?
Brief Answer: The former employee was not personally or directly involved in this
particular application, and no violation of Section 25-4-105(3)(e),
Miss. Code of 1972, is likely to occur. The former employee may
have gained nonpublic information which could be used in violation
of Section 25-4-105(5), and an appearance of impropriety could
arise under Section 25-4-101. Those concerns could prompt the
state agency to deny the application of this former employee.
The Mississippi Ethics Commission issued this opinion on the date shown above in
accordance with Section 25-4-17(i), Mississippi Code of 1972, as reflected upon its minutes of
even date. The Commission is empowered to interpret and opine only upon Article IV, Section
109, Mississippi Constitution of 1890, and Article 3, Chapter 4, Title 25, Mississippi Code of 1972.
This opinion does not interpret or offer protection from liability for any other laws, rules or
regulations. The Commission based this opinion solely on the facts and circumstances provided
by the requestor as restated herein. The protection from liability provided under Section 25-4-17(i)
is limited to the individual who requested this opinion and to the accuracy and completeness of
these facts.
I. LAW
The pertinent Ethics in Government Laws to be considered here are as follows:

Section 25-4-101, Miss. Code of 1972.
The legislature declares that elective and public office and employment is a public
trust and any effort to realize personal gain through official conduct, other than as
provided by law, or as a natural consequence of the employment or position, is a
violation of that trust. Therefore, public servants shall endeavor to pursue a course
of conduct which will not raise suspicion among the public that they are likely to
be engaged in acts that are in violation of this trust and which will not reflect
unfavorably upon the state and local governments.
Section 25-4-103, Miss. Code of 1972.
(c) “Business” means any corporation, partnership, sole proprietorship, firm,
enterprise, franchise, association, organization, holding company, self-employed
individual, joint stock company, receivership, trust or other legal entity or
undertaking organized for economic gain, a nonprofit corporation or other such
entity, association or organization receiving public funds.
(e) “Compensation” means money or thing of value received, or to be received,
from any person for services rendered.
(l) “Pecuniary benefit” means benefit in the form of money, property, commercial
interests or anything else the primary significance of which is economic gain.
Expenses associated with social occasions afforded public servants shall not be
deemed a pecuniary benefit.
(m) “Person” means any individual, firm, business, corporation, association,
partnership, union or other legal entity, and where appropriate a governmental
entity.
(p) “Public servant” means:
(i) Any elected or appointed official of the government;
(ii) Any officer, director, commissioner, supervisor, chief, head, agent or
employee of the government or any agency thereof, or of any public entity
created by or under the laws of the state of Mississippi or created by an
agency or governmental entity thereof, any of which is funded by public
funds or which expends, authorizes or recommends the use of public funds;
or
(iii) Any individual who receives a salary, per diem or expenses paid in
whole or in part out of funds authorized to be expended by the government.
Section 25-4-105, Miss. Code of 1972.
(3) No public servant shall:

(e) Perform any service for any compensation for any person or business
after termination of his office or employment in relation to any case,
decision, proceeding or application with respect to which he was directly
concerned or in which he personally participated during the period of his
service or employment.
(5) No person may intentionally use or disclose information gained in the course of
or by reason of his official position or employment as a public servant in any way
that could result in pecuniary benefit for himself, any relative, or any other person,
if the information has not been communicated to the public or is not public
information.
II. FACTS
Facts provided by the requestor are set forth below, with identifying information redacted, and
are considered a part of this opinion.
[A state agency] respectfully requests an advisory opinion pursuant to Miss. Code
Ann. § 25-4-17 regarding the post-government employment restrictions contained
in Miss. Code Ann. § 25-4-105(3)(e). The agency seeks guidance on whether a
former [agency] employee’s participation in [a particular agency program] Request
for Applications (“RFA”) process presents a prohibited conflict of interest under
the Ethics in Government Law.
The individual at issue (“Former Employee”) served as Director of [a program].
While [that program] is not part of the [the program in question here], both
programs operate within the [same office of the agency], share related subject-
matter areas involving [similar] services, and coordinate on various programmatic
matters.
The Former Employee applied to become [a] service provider [in this program]
through [the agency’s] RFA process. At the time she submitted her application, she
was still an [agency] employee, although she had already tendered her resignation.
As part of the RFA process, applicants must complete a conflict-of-interest
disclosure. In her initial submission, the Former Employee indicated that she was
not an [agency] employee. However, [agency] records confirm that at the time her
conflict-of-interest responses were submitted, she was still employed by [the
agency].
Based on her inaccurate conflict-of-interest disclosure and because she submitted
[a] provider application while still employed by the agency, [the agency]
determined that her application was disqualified. However, following her
separation from [the agency], the Former Employee withdrew her initial …
provider application and subsequently resubmitted an application with the same
substantive responses. At the time of the resubmission, she was no longer employed
by [the agency].

[The agency] seeks an advisory opinion on whether the Former Employee’s
participation in the … RFA process, whether through her initial application
submitted while still employed or through her post-employment resubmission,
implicates the Mississippi Ethics in Government Law and the post-government
employment restrictions contained in Miss. Code Ann. § 25-4-105(3)(e).
Specifically, [the agency] seeks clarification on:
1. Whether the Former Employee’s application to become [a] service provider
constitutes a matter that is prohibited under § 25-4-105(3)(e) based on her
prior role as director of … a program that is organizationally separate from,
but located within the same office as, the [program in question].
2. Whether her resubmission of the same application after her employment
ended remains prohibited, given that her initial submission occurred while
she was still an [agency] employee.
3. Whether her inaccurate completion of the conflict-of-interest disclosure
affects the analysis under § 25-4-105(3)(e).
[The agency] respectfully requests an advisory opinion addressing the questions
identified above and appreciates any guidance the Commission can provide
regarding how the agency should proceed with evaluating the Former Employee’s
… provider application in compliance with the Mississippi Ethics in Government
Law.
In response to questions from the commission’s staff, the requestor provided the following
supplemental information.
This individual submitted [the] initial application to become [a service provider]
while still employed by the agency. Although employed by [the agency], [the
employee] would not have been involved in the review, scoring, or award process.
[The agency] disqualified [the] initial application for answering a question in the
negative regarding her current affiliation with the agency. Those reviewing her
application noted she was still employed by the agency at the time of submission
and disqualified her application. This individual subsequently withdrew her
application and reapplied for the same program after she was terminated from the
agency.
Her initial application was submitted by her business entity, [a limited liability
company]. [I]t is not a single-member LLC owned entirely by this individual. We
believe the other member listed is her husband.
We are not entirely sure what non-public information she could have access to. It
is possible that she may have been involved in or present for discussions during …
staff meetings where information regarding the … program [in question here] was
shared that might not have been made available to the general public.

III. ANALYSIS
The Ethics Commission cannot opine on past action, and this opinion neither condones nor
comments on any past action which may be referenced in the facts provided above.
Section 25-4-105(3)(e), Miss. Code of 1972, addresses successive government and private
sector employment. Section 25-4-105(3)(e) will not necessarily prohibit a former public servant
from being employed by an entity which contracts with his or her former government employer.
The law merely prohibits the former public servant from working for pay in the private sector on
any matter in which he or she was directly or personally involved while working for the
government.
Therefore, if the former public servant was not directly concerned with and did not
personally participate in the matter in question, then the former public servant may legally accept
payment from the private entity to work on that matter. Elec. Data Sys. Corp. v. Miss. Div. of
Medicaid, 853 So.2d 1192, 1204, 1205 (¶¶ 35, 39) (Miss. 2003). If the former public servant was
directly concerned with and did personally participate in the matter in question, then the private
entity may still contract with the government, but the former public servant may not be paid in
relation to that matter. Id.
Here the matter in question is the application to become a service provider to the state
agency at which the applicant was formerly employed. There are no facts to indicate the applicant
had any personal or direct involvement in this application, especially since it was submitted after
the applicant terminated employment with the agency. Consequently, it appears that no violation
of Section 25-4-105(3)(e) will occur if the former employee’s LLC becomes a service provider to
the state agency.
Section 25-4-105(5) prohibits a public servant from intentionally using or disclosing
information gained through government employment in any way that could result in pecuniary
benefit for himself, any relative, or any other person, if the information is not public. The facts
indicate the former state employee may have gained nonpublic information during the period of
state employment which could now be used to gain a competitive advantage in the application
process or some other monetary benefit. The potential for a violation of Section 25-4-105(5) is of
concern in this matter and should give the agency pause.
Additionally, Section 25-4-101 admonishes all current and former public servants to pursue
a course of conduct which does not raise suspicion among the public that they are violating the
public trust or which reflects unfavorably upon the government. The public might reasonably
suspect a former state employee who applies to be a service provider to the same office in which
he or she was formerly employed may do so to realize personal gain. The potential for a violation
of Section 25-4-105(5) coupled with the possible appearance of impropriety under Section 25-4-
101 could prompt the state agency to deny the application of this former employee.
